analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top individual income tax rate and the corporate rate to 33%.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lowered federal income tax rates for both individuals and corporations. The top individual rate would have fallen from 39.6% to 33% over several years, the top corporate rate from 35% to 33%, and the corporate minimum tax rate from 20% to 19%. Because tax rates are graduated, the largest dollar savings would have gone to households and companies with the biggest profits, while the federal government would have collected less money overall.
analysis.who_benefits: The clearest beneficiaries would have been households with taxable income above the top brackets and corporations with large profits, since the top individual rate would have dropped from 39.6% to 33% and the corporate rate from 35% to 33% over several years [S3]. Every filer would have seen a small rate cut, but the value of a rate cut grows with the amount of income taxed at the top rates, so the savings would have been concentrated at the top [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the individual tax tables with lower rates, starting at a 14% first bracket in 2002 and phasing down to a 10%, 15%, 25%, and 33% structure by 2006, replacing the prior 39.6% top rate [S3].
The corporate rate on income over $75,000 would drop from 35% to 33% (34% in 2002 and 2003), and the corporate alternative minimum tax rate would fall from 20% to 19% [S3].

Conforming amendments apply the lower 33% rate to the personal-holding-company tax and the accumulated-earnings-tax rate references in sections 531 and 541, and adjust withholding and backup-withholding rates to match the new brackets [S3].
The bill updates the inflation-indexing base years used to set bracket thresholds and other dollar limits from the early 1990s to 2000-2001 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the federal government would have collected less revenue from the top individual brackets and from corporations. That shortfall would have been borne broadly, either through larger deficits passed on to future taxpayers or through less money available for federal programs and services. Households with little or no income taxed at the top rates would have seen minimal direct benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and service programs, via lost revenue

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top individual rate from 39.6% to 33% and the corporate rate from 35% to 33% reduces federal revenue, and because the biggest rates apply only to the largest incomes and profits, the largest dollar savings go to the highest earners and the most profitable companies [S3].
The bill includes no offsetting revenue increase or spending cut, so the lost revenue would have added to federal deficits or crowded out other spending [S3].

A good-faith supporter's honest concession: freezing the inflation adjustment on the lowest two brackets through 2006 (section 1(f)(7)(A) of the text) means modest-income filers would not have gotten the same bracket-widening benefit as filers in higher brackets during the phase-in [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Every filer and every corporation would have paid a lower rate, but the design stacks the benefit at the top: the rate cuts are deepest in the brackets that only high earners and profitable corporations touch, and there is no pay-for. The cost is a broad one — lower federal revenue affecting everyone through deficits or reduced services — while the direct gain is concentrated. The bill also offers nothing targeted at low- and middle-income households beyond the small cut in the bottom brackets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on March 6, 2001 and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No other member signed on: the bill had 0 cosponsors for its entire life [S4].
The action history shows only introduction, introductory remarks, and referral — no markup, no committee report, and no floor action ever followed [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2003 with the bill still stalled in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal revenue base was not reduced by these cuts — the biggest would-be winners, high earners and corporations, did not get the lower rates, and taxpayers broadly avoided the revenue loss it would have caused.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal revenue base, not high earners

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor on March 6, 2001.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled action on it; it was never reported out.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so neither party ever took a recorded position on it [S4].

industries.note: The bill cuts the top corporate rate from 35% to 33% and the corporate minimum tax rate from 20% to 19%, directly reducing what the most profitable companies owe [S3]. Their gain comes from federal revenue that would otherwise fund programs or reduce deficits, so their interest runs against ordinary taxpayers' in this bill.

The top individual rate falls from 39.6% to 33% over several years; since the largest brackets apply only to the largest incomes, the biggest dollar savings go to households at the top [S3]. That saving is mirrored by lost federal revenue borne by everyone.
